sections.report:
**Walk (working notes): The whole piece**
- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? Yes. It is Brightpath's analytics overview: visits, sign-ups and conversion for the last 12 weeks.
- Do the main image and the headline make one idea together? Yes. "Visits by channel" sits over a multi-line chart. The chart has no legend and no axes, so you can't tell which line is which channel, but that belongs to Charts and data.
- Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job? Yes at the level of the whole piece. The unlabelled gridlines belong to Charts and data.
- Do type, colours and shapes share one mood and era? Yes.
- Is the copy finished, with no placeholders or typos? Yes.
- Does each kind of element look the same everywhere? Yes. The three KPI cards match, and so do the green delta lines.
- Do colours, shapes and directions carry the right mood? Yes.
- Does each heading name what its section holds? Yes. "Overview" is generic, but it is accurate for a summary page.

No line answered `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(For the director: the biggest problem on this image is outside this section. The "Visits by channel" chart (about x 49–1231, y 283–758) has no legend, no y-axis values and no x-axis labels. The viewer can't tell which channel is blue, orange or green, or read any value or week. A band about 75 px tall under the baseline (y ~684–758) is empty where x-axis labels would normally go. The data critic should cover this. It also makes the largest element on the page carry only one message, "three things trend up", which takes away from the whole piece.)

**What's working.**
- The three KPI cards (y 142–262) give one sentence's worth of meaning at a glance: big number, plain label, delta with a stated comparison period ("vs previous 12 weeks"). A first-time viewer knows what the page is for within seconds.
- One quiet, consistent visual language (neutral greys, a single sans family, matching card radius and border, green used only for positive deltas) makes the page read as one product, not a collage.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The empty band under the chart baseline and the missing axis text could be a render or load failure, not the design. Check in a live browser whether axis labels and a legend appear.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No.
   - **Where:** The three KPI cards (about x 48–1232, y 142–262) are identical: same box, same roughly 28 px bold number, same green delta line.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The eye starts at 184,220 only because it is on the left, then moves across to 3,912 and 2.12% without being told which one is the story. Below them, the chart (y 282–758) is the largest area on the page, but its only claim on attention is three coloured lines with a small title. The viewer leaves with "everything is up a little" and no headline.
   - **Why:** This is the case the rule names: three elements of the same size, weight and colour strength competing to be seen first (Tschichold, *The New Typography*; Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual*: contrast of much against little).
   - **Fix:** If one metric is what this team is judged on (probably sign-ups or conversion rate), make it clearly the first thing seen and set the other two back by size, for example a wider card or a larger number. If the three metrics really are equal peers, keep the row as it is and give the page a lead some other way, such as a title on the chart that states what it shows.
   - **Kind:** Convention. Equal KPI tiles are a common dashboard pattern, so this costs less here than on a poster.
   - **Weight:** Minor.
2. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. There are three places:
   - **"Overview" against the KPI numbers.** The page title "Overview" (about 24 px bold, y about 105) and the KPI numbers (about 28 px bold, y about 203) are a few pixels apart in size, with the same weight and colour. They read as one level with a slip in it, so the title does not clearly sit above the cards. A dashboard's numbers may well be bigger than its page title (Refactoring UI), but the gap has to look deliberate.
   - **The brand and the chart title.** "Brightpath Analytics" (about 17 px semibold, top bar) and "Visits by channel" (about 17 px semibold, y about 313) look the same size and weight, although one is the app's name and the other is a section heading.
   - **Card labels and deltas.** The card labels ("Visits", "Sign-ups", about 14 px grey) and the deltas (about 13 px green) are almost the same size. Here colour carries the difference, so the cost is small.
   - **Why:** Sizes that close look picked one at a time, not taken from a scale (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 3.1.1, p. 45). A difference of one step looks like an accident, not a choice (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8).
   - **Fix:** Use a smaller set of sizes with clear steps between them. Either make "Overview" clearly larger than the numbers, or drop it to a quieter label and let the numbers lead on purpose. Move the chart title or the brand onto its own step, and set the labels and deltas at one shared size.
   - **Kind:** Defect, though a mild one.
   - **Weight:** Minor.

**What's working.**
- **Headings differ by weight as well as size.** Every heading-level line ("Overview", "Visits by channel", the KPI numbers) is bold against regular-weight labels and grey secondary text, so the levels separate by more than size. That is why the hierarchy still holds despite the close sizes.
- **Clear reading order between bands.** The quiet top bar, then the KPI row, then the chart run top to bottom with generous gaps, so the order between bands is never in doubt, even though nothing inside a band leads.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element stands above the rest; distinct text levels with no near-equal sizes), 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?"** No. The chart title "Visits by channel" starts at about x=71, while the card labels above it ("Visits", "Sign-ups", "Conversion rate") start at about x=69. That means the chart panel's inner padding (~23 px) doesn't match the cards' (~21 px). The first series point at x≈143 also sits about 22 px inside the plot's left edge at x≈121, so the lines don't start on the axis or line up with anything above. The viewer won't name the problem, but a 2 px miss on the page's main left text axis makes the build look slightly hand-placed. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I) says a placement that is neither clearly on a line nor clearly off it makes the eye waver. The catalog marks that the point is not confirmed in Samara. Fix: give the panels and cards one inner padding so all panel titles share one left edge. Either start the series on the plot edge or make the inset clearly deliberate. Defect. Weight: minor.
2. **"Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?"** No. Inside the chart panel there are two leftover bands: a ~70 px empty strip left of the plot (x≈49–121, y≈360–685) and a ~75 px empty band under the baseline (y≈685–758). They look like room kept for y-axis and x-axis labels that aren't there. As drawn, the plot floats off-centre inside its card with dead margins on two sides, and that space does no work. This is not the page's main white space: the grey page margins are gathered and fine. Ruder (*Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts") asks for empty space gathered so it creates tension, not left over. This is fine if the axis labels are supposed to fill those bands and simply didn't render in this capture. Then the missing labels are the issue, and that belongs to Charts and data. If the bands are meant to be empty, close them so the plot fills the panel. Defect. Weight: minor, though missing axis labels would be major under Charts and data.

**What's working.**
- **One grid holds the page.** The three KPI cards (x≈48–428, 450–830, 852–1231) sit on equal ~22 px gutters. The chart panel spans exactly the outer edges of the card row, and the brand name and "Last 12 weeks" line up with those same outer edges. The page reads as one system, so keep the shared 48 px margin and the single gutter.
- **Space shows the groups.** Inside each card, the label, figure and delta are packed tight, about 10–15 px apart. The cards are separated by ~22 px and the page margin is wider still. Each metric reads as one unit at a glance, so keep that ratio.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the three-card row reflows at narrower widths (whether it stacks or squeezes) matters for a dashboard, but it can't be seen in a still. The crop script also didn't run because Bash was denied, so I judged from the whole 1280×800 image. At that size the 2 px offsets above are estimates by eye.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (no near-misses of a few pixels; empty space gathered, not scattered)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye goes to the three large numbers (184,220 / 3,912 / 2.12%), then down to the three lines in the chart. It reads as a growth or marketing analytics dashboard for a team checking traffic and conversion over the last 12 weeks. It feels calm, clean and generic. Assumed job: give a marketer a quick answer to "how are we doing versus last period, and which channel is driving it."

Text:
1. Body text large enough: yes. There are no paragraphs, and the labels look about 14 px.
2. Captions and labels large enough: yes. The green delta lines look about 12–13 px and are crisp in the crop.
3. Plain reading face: yes.
4. One typeface plan: yes. There is one sans family, in regular and bold.
5. Small text weight holds up: yes.
6. Contrast: yes. The grey card labels and the green deltas both look comfortably above 4.5:1 on white.
7. Text over images: yes, there is none.
8–17. Paragraph lines, leading, multi-line headings, flush left, justification, rag, widows, line breaks, paragraph marks, hanging punctuation: yes. There are no paragraphs, and every heading fits on one line.
18. Long text chunked: yes.
19. Mixed case: yes.
20. Emphasis changes one thing: yes.
21. Large headings set tighter: yes. "Overview" and the figures look set normally for display.
22. Kerning: yes.
23. Lower-case tracking: yes.
24. Capitals letterspaced: yes, there are no strings of capitals.
25. Ligatures: yes. Nothing at large size needs one.
26. Real cuts: yes.
27. Quotes and dashes: yes, there are none.
28. Tabular figures: yes. The KPI figures sit in separate cards, not in a column.
29. Real type: yes.
30. Nothing clipped: yes.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Type is limited to one sans family.** Size and weight do the work: bold for the figures, regular grey for labels, small green for deltas. Each card reads in one pass: what it is, the number, then the change. Keep it to these three levels per card when revising.
- **The deltas are written out in full.** They say "+6.1% vs previous 12 weeks", and conversion uses "+0.1 pts", not a misleading "%". The viewer doesn't have to guess what the change is measured against, or whether a rate change is relative or absolute. That matters because these are numbers people repeat in meetings.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

Walk (working notes). Color, outside charts and controls:
- Small palette: yes. Neutral grays, plus green for status. The three series hues belong to the chart.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes.
- Value range holds in grayscale: yes. The white cards on a pale gray ground are a small step, but the borders carry the structure.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. Outside the chart, nothing warm competes.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The three green deltas match.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. Green marks gains, and all three deltas are positive.
- Color backed by a label or sign: yes outside the chart, since each delta has a "+" sign and the "vs previous 12 weeks" text. The chart's series are told apart by color alone with no legend, but that gets filed under Charts and data.
- Dark theme: yes, because it doesn't apply (light theme).

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 has no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Note for the director: there is one color problem, but it sits inside the chart. In "Visits by channel" (about x 120–1200, y 360–690), the blue, orange and green lines are told apart only by color. There is no legend, no direct labels and no axis labels, so a viewer can't tell which line is which channel. Under this checklist's rule it gets filed under Charts and data, not Color. I'd weight it major. The fix is to put a label at the right end of each line.

**What's working.**
- **Restrained palette.** Outside the chart the page is neutral: white cards on a pale gray ground with near-black type. The only hue is green on the KPI deltas. So the chart's three colored lines are the only strong color on the page, and the eye goes to the data rather than the chrome.
- **Status color is backed by text.** Each delta ("+6.1% vs previous 12 weeks", y ≈ 234) uses green for the usual meaning of a gain. It also has a "+" sign and a comparison phrase, so the meaning doesn't rely on color alone.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, or graphic marks. "Brightpath Analytics" at top left is plain bold text, not a drawn logo, so it belongs under Text. The line chart belongs under Charts and data.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies (three KPI cards and one multi-line chart, "Visits by channel").

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart name what its marks show, with axis values, units, and series labels?** No. The chart (about x 70–1200, y 340–700) has five faint gridlines with no y values, no week or date labels under the baseline at y≈684, and no channel names anywhere. A viewer can see three rising lines but can't tell which channel is which, how many visits any line stands for, or which week a dip falls in (such as the blue dip at x≈805). They also can't tell whether the gaps between the lines are large or small, because the y range isn't shown. They can't check the lines against the 184,220 total in the card above either. The chart is decoration until it's labelled. Fix: add y tick values in visits on the gridlines and week labels on the x axis, and name each line. Defect (Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 2; Few, *Show Me the Numbers*). Weight: major.
2. **Is each series label placed at its data rather than in a separate legend?** No. There is no legend at all, and no label at the line ends (around x 1185, at y≈411 blue, y≈518 orange, y≈588 green). The fix that solves finding 1 best is a channel name written in the line's colour just right of each endpoint. There's empty space there inside the card (x 1185–1230), and the viewer never has to look back and forth to decode colours. Convention (Tufte; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*). Weight: major. It's the same gap as finding 1, so the director may merge them.
3. **Can each chart's series be told apart without color vision, by labels, shapes, or a color-blind-safe palette such as Okabe-Ito?** No. The three series differ only in hue, all with the same stroke weight and style. With deuteranopia, the orange line and the green line are a common confusion pair. Today they can only be told apart because they don't overlap. Direct labels at the line ends (finding 2) fix this too, and WCAG 1.4.1 expects that. Defect (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 *Use of Color*). Weight: minor, because the lines sit in separate bands and labels would remove the issue.
4. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** No. "Visits by channel" (x 71, y 313) only names the topic. The dashboard's one sentence of interpretation could go here: which channel drives the +6.1%, or which one is flat (the green line rises only slightly). Fix: a title or subtitle that states what changed, such as which channel grew most over the 12 weeks. Taste and common sense: no approved source states this. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Every headline number has a comparison. All three cards show a delta against the previous 12 weeks, and the conversion card correctly uses "pts" rather than "%" for a change in a rate, which avoids a common misreading.
- The chart has very little ink that isn't data. Gridlines are pale, there's no chart border inside the card, and there are no markers or effects. The three lines sit in separate bands and never cross, so each can be followed on its own.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether hovering the chart shows a tooltip with values and dates. It only partly makes up for missing axes, since a glanceable dashboard shouldn't need hovering to be read.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 12 yes, 4 no (axis values, units, and series labels; labels at the data; series distinguishable without colour; title states the finding)

**Section.** Interface: applies. This is an analytics dashboard, and "Last 12 weeks" in the header is in the spot where users expect a date-range control. There are no other visible controls.

**Findings**
1. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** — No. "Last 12 weeks" (about x 1133–1232, y 20–38, in the top right of the header) is set as plain grey text, the same as a caption. It has no border, chevron, calendar icon or button shape. Analytics products put the date-range picker in that exact spot as a dropdown button, so users will look there to change the period. They will find text that does not look clickable, and they either won't try it or will click and guess. If it is a picker, it needs to look like one: a bordered button with a chevron, the usual pattern in Material and Apple HIG. If it is only a label, it is fine, but then the dashboard has no way to change the period at all (see 3). Norman (signifiers) and Krug both make this point: things you can click must look clickable. Defect if it is interactive. Weight: major.
2. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step, progress, or loading?** — No. The page title "Overview" (48, 105) implies there are other views, but the header (y 0–58) has only the product name. There are no tabs, side nav or current-page marker, so the user cannot tell whether other views exist or how to reach them. The dashboard also says nothing about how fresh the data is: no "Updated 2 h ago" and no date range in real dates. In an analytics tool the user then cannot tell whether 184,220 visits counts through today or through some earlier cut-off. Fix: add the navigation with "Overview" marked as current, or drop the heading if this really is the only view, and add the data's last-updated time or the actual date span beside the period control. Defect (Nielsen 1, visibility of system status). Weight: minor.
3. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** — No. On a dashboard the frequent actions are changing the period, comparing against another range, filtering by channel and drilling into a metric. Nothing on the screen offers any of them. The KPI cards (y 143–261) and the chart card (y 283–758) look static, and the chart has no channel toggle or filter. Fix: make the period control visible (finding 1). Make the KPI cards or the chart's series lines visibly clickable to drill in, or add a channel filter next to "Visits by channel". Convention (Nielsen 7). Weight: minor, but it rises if this screen is meant for repeat analysts rather than a glance-only summary.

**What's working.**
- Nothing competes for attention. There are no stray buttons, banners or pop-ups, so the KPIs and the chart get the whole screen. That suits a glance-first overview.
- Each KPI card says exactly what its change is measured against: "vs previous 12 weeks", and "pts" for the conversion rate rather than a misleading percent of a percent. The user never has to remember the comparison base.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether "Last 12 weeks" is interactive, and if it is, what its hover, focus and open states look like.
- Whether the chart has hover tooltips that name each series and value. With no legend on screen, that decides whether the chart can be read at all. The missing legend itself belongs to the data section.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 30 yes, 3 no (controls look like what they do; shows where the user is and what is happening; shortcuts for frequent actions), 0 unsure
